coherence.reasons: Both run a clean chain from market to unit economics to customers to cash to the software alternative, and each executive summary maps onto its slides. Y's five sections mirror its summary exactly, but its Zipcart page sits in the body without feeding the summary. X adds a page testing the founders' three claims one by one, and its summary ends in explicit board decisions that the options and trigger pages support. X's sensitivity pages (waterfall, generous combinations) directly support the summary claim that the plan needs every input above the best site. The difference is small.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (do not launch, scale the software) and both set conditions for reopening the operator question. X weighs the alternatives more rigorously. It costs a one-store pilot ($0.6M capex plus about $2.0M a year of losses, runway floor breached around month 8) and explains that scaling it brings back the full plan. It also notes the core business reaches the runway floor in about 18 months regardless, so burn must fall, and it proposes a capital-light design-partner offer with pipeline grocers. Y dismisses the smaller test in one line (the pop-up already lost money) with no costing. Y's headline for the software option uses the full 37-grocer pipeline ($3.6M ARR), which it admits is an upper bound; X leads with the 9 late-stage deals. X's triggers are also more operational (two quarters of positive contribution with promotions at or below 6%).

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: −$6.17 at median, −$1.76 at best composite, −$12.57 for the pop-up, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, and −$18.2M a year for nine stores at median. X goes further on the critical evidence. It gives the 41.5% CAGR, a one-at-a-time and waterfall sensitivity (density explains only about a fifth of the gap), a best-of-everything case (−$0.08), required density (about 6,400 orders a day) and rider-pay sensitivity ($0.29–0.42 per $1 an hour). Most importantly, it quantifies the Zipcart playbook on a median store (−$1.05 after the 14% volume loss), which matches the key. Y treats Zipcart only qualitatively (fee, promotion cut, volume loss, 'five times that profit with no fee') and never applies the fee to Parcelbird's economics. Y's additions are correct and useful: a $63 break-even basket at median costs, 43.2% of the loss arising before store cost, and a 28-month payback. X's one overreach is 'nothing in the evidence supports +$2': it did not test the fee at best observed density, which would be positive. X also flags its own assumptions and inferences (channel conflict, pop-up growth path) more explicitly.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while keeping the part the evidence supports (market growth). X does this explicitly: it splits the founders' view into three claims, upholds the growth claim, and rejects the 'we run stores better' claim (the 14 sites already run on its software, and its own pop-up did worse than the median) and the density claim (density is only about $1.75 of the $8.19 gap). It also tests the evidence that partly supports the founders, the Zipcart fee, and shows it still loses at median density. Y accepts the growth claim, notes there is no Midwest data, and calls the Zipcart proof point thin. But it does not address the operating-edge claim directly or quantify whether the fee could rescue the economics.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with correct core calculations. X serves the board better on the points the founders are likely to contest. It rebuts each founder claim directly, shows which assumptions carry the plan, quantifies the Zipcart fee scenario and the one-store pilot, and flags that burn must fall even without a launch. It closes with concrete decisions and measurable reopen triggers. Y is sound and adds a useful break-even basket, but it is thinner on the Zipcart counter-evidence and the pilot alternative, and it headlines an upper-bound pipeline figure.
